description: Vitamin A derivative that speeds cell turnover, softens fine lines and unclogs pores. Introduce slowly; causes irritation and sun sensitivity.
One conversion step closer to retinoic acid than retinol, so it works faster at lower strengths.
The gentlest and weakest retinoid ester. Good for beginners, limited results.
Hybrid retinoid that is more stable than retinol with comparable efficacy.
Retinoic acid ester that binds receptors directly with notably less irritation than retinol.
Prescription-grade retinoid now sold over the counter for acne. Highly effective on comedones.
Plant-derived compound with retinol-like effects on lines and tone, without the irritation or sun sensitivity.
Smallest AHA, so it penetrates deepest. Strong on texture, dullness and dark spots; also the most irritating AHA.
Gentler AHA that exfoliates while also acting as a humectant. A good first acid for dry skin.
Large-molecule AHA, the mildest of the family. Suits sensitive and acne-prone skin.
Mild AHA from apples, usually a supporting acid in a blend.
Grape-derived AHA, typically used to buffer and support stronger acids.
Almost always present in tiny amounts to adjust pH rather than to exfoliate.
Oil-soluble acid that clears inside the pore. The single most useful active for blackheads and congested, oily skin.
Gentler salicylic acid derivative common in K-beauty, usually at 2 to 4 percent.
Lipophilic salicylic derivative that exfoliates the very surface. Gentler than standard BHA.
Natural source of salicin. Far milder than salicylic acid and often used more for marketing than effect.
Large polyhydroxy acid that exfoliates gently and hydrates. A safe bet for sensitive skin.
PHA with antioxidant and strong water-binding properties.
Unusually versatile: calms redness and rosacea, fades post-acne marks and is antibacterial. Well tolerated.
Kills acne bacteria directly. Very effective on inflamed acne; drying, and it bleaches fabric.
Antibacterial and keratolytic acne treatment. Effective but notoriously smelly and drying.
The gold-standard vitamin C. Brightens, fades pigment and boosts sun protection. Unstable and low pH, so it can sting.
Stable, pH-neutral vitamin C derivative. Milder, and also mildly antibacterial.
Gentle stable vitamin C derivative suited to sensitive skin.
Stable vitamin C derivative that converts slowly on skin.
Stable vitamin C derivative compatible with both water and oil phases, popular in serums.
Oil-soluble vitamin C that penetrates well and does not sting. Expensive.
Stable oil-soluble vitamin C ester.
Workhorse active: regulates oil, strengthens the barrier, evens tone and reduces redness. Plays well with nearly everything.
Targets dark spots by inhibiting pigment production, without the irritation of hydroquinone.
Naturally derived pigment inhibitor, gentler and slower than hydroquinone.
Especially effective on melasma and stubborn post-inflammatory pigmentation.
Fungal-derived brightener for dark spots. Can sensitise with prolonged use.
Antioxidant marketed for brightening; topical evidence is modest.
Binds many times its weight in water. Hydrates the surface; seal it with a moisturizer or it can dry skin in low humidity.
The salt form of hyaluronic acid. Smaller molecule, absorbs more readily.
Low-molecular-weight HA fragments that reach slightly deeper layers.
Modified HA that adheres to skin longer than the standard form.
The most reliable humectant in skincare. Cheap, proven, and suits every skin type.
Lightweight humectant and solvent that thins textures and aids penetration.
Plant-derived glycol used as a gentler alternative to propylene glycol.
Effective humectant and penetration enhancer, but a known contact allergen for a minority of people.
Hydrates while boosting preservative performance.
Low-irritation glycol used to carry actives.
Beet-derived osmolyte that hydrates and buffers irritation from actives.
Hydrates and visibly calms irritation. A staple of barrier-repair and post-active products.
Hydrates at low percentages and softens rough, thickened skin at high ones.
Sugar that protects cells against dehydration stress.
A component of the natural moisturizing factor already present in skin.
Calms and softens. A quiet workhorse in sensitive-skin formulas.
Replenishes the lipid mortar between skin cells. Central to barrier repair.
Barrier ceramide, usually paired with NP and EOP.
Long-chain ceramide important for barrier integrity.
Common barrier-repair ceramide.
Ceramide precursor with mild antimicrobial action.
One of the three essential barrier lipids, alongside ceramides and fatty acids.
Lightweight, stable oil that mimics skin sebum. Non-greasy and tolerated by almost everyone.
Light, silky coconut-derived emollient used across almost all textures.
Forms a breathable film that slows water loss and gives a smooth finish.
Volatile silicone giving instant slip that then evaporates.
Silicone elastomer that blurs pores and gives a soft-focus finish.
The most effective occlusive available, cutting water loss by over 95 percent. Heavy but non-comedogenic.
Highly refined and inert occlusive. Contrary to reputation, cosmetic-grade mineral oil is non-comedogenic.
Extremely effective at sealing moisture, but a relatively common contact allergen.
Rich fatty butter for dry and compromised skin. Can feel heavy on oily skin.
Highly occlusive plant oil and strongly comedogenic. A common trigger for facial breakouts.
Very light-feeling emollient, but among the most pore-clogging ingredients in common use.
Silky emollient with a high comedogenic rating.
Liquid wax closely resembling human sebum. A balanced choice for most skin types.
Rich in linoleic acid and natural vitamin A precursors. Popular for tone and scarring.
High-linoleic oil that supports the barrier without clogging pores.
Vitamin E-rich oil, light enough for most skin types.
Oleic-heavy oil. Nourishing on dry skin, but it can aggravate acne-prone skin.
Light, high-linoleic oil that absorbs quickly.
Mild nourishing oil, moderately occlusive.
Calms redness and supports barrier repair. The signature K-beauty soothing ingredient.
Purified centella fraction, strongly anti-inflammatory.
Centella compound linked to wound healing and collagen support.
Anti-inflammatory centella acid.
Centella acid included in cica complexes.
EGCG-rich antioxidant that calms skin and helps regulate oil.
Calms redness and gently fades pigment via glabridin.
Oat- or yeast-derived polysaccharide that hydrates and calms reactive skin.
Clinically recognised anti-itch and barrier-soothing ingredient for eczema-prone skin.
Oat-derived soother used in sensitive-skin formulas.
Chamomile-derived anti-inflammatory.
Combined soothing and hydrating complex.
Regulates sebum and has mild antibacterial action.
Used in trace amounts to raise formula pH. Harmless as formulated.
Fat-soluble antioxidant that also stabilises oils in a formula. Works synergistically with vitamin C.
Stable vitamin E ester, converted slowly on skin.
Plant antioxidant that stabilises vitamin C and E and boosts their photoprotection.
Polyphenol antioxidant with anti-inflammatory action.
Cellular antioxidant that declines with age.
INCI name for coenzyme Q10.
Potent algae-derived carotenoid antioxidant.
Signal peptide that encourages collagen production.
Anti-inflammatory signal peptide, usually paired with Tripeptide-1.
Marketed as a topical alternative to injectables for expression lines. Evidence is limited.
Copper peptide associated with wound healing and firmness.
Sits on the surface as a hydrating film. Topical collagen cannot replace your own.
Korea-approved functional anti-wrinkle ingredient. Well tolerated.
K-beauty staple prized for hydration, healing and post-acne marks.
Probiotic ferment linked to barrier support and repair.
Yeast ferment used for radiance and texture. Can trigger fungal acne in some people.
Ferment filtrate used for brightening and hydration.
Probiotic ferment supporting the skin microbiome.
Traditional brightening and softening ingredient in K-beauty.
INCI name for rice extract.
Bee-derived resin with antibacterial and healing properties.
Natural humectant with mild antibacterial action.
Broad-spectrum mineral filter covering UVA and UVB. Very low irritation, so it suits sensitive and reactive skin.
Mineral filter strongest in UVB. Often paired with zinc oxide for full coverage.
The main UVA filter available in the US. Needs stabilising partners or it degrades in sunlight.
UVB filter that also helps dissolve other filters.
UVB filter used to stabilise avobenzone. An occasional contact allergen.
Widely used UVB filter, restricted in some regions over reef concerns.
Modern photostable UVA filter available in Asia and Europe but not the US.
Excellent photostable broad-spectrum filter. Common in Asian and European sunscreens.
Highly efficient UVB filter used at low percentages.
Undisclosed scent blend and the leading cause of cosmetic contact allergy. Best avoided on sensitive or compromised skin.
European labelling term for fragrance. Same irritation considerations apply.
Citrus fragrance component and declarable EU allergen. Oxidises into a stronger sensitiser.
Floral fragrance component and declarable EU allergen.
Rose-scented fragrance component and declarable EU allergen.
Fragrance component and declarable EU allergen.
Clove-like fragrance component and declarable EU allergen.
Lemon-scented fragrance component and declarable EU allergen.
Gives a fast, weightless finish but can dry and irritate over time, especially high in the ingredient list.
Drying solvent when present at high concentration.
Essential oil that is cytotoxic to skin cells in lab studies and a frequent sensitiser.
Antibacterial essential oil used for acne, but a common sensitiser at higher concentrations.
Phototoxic citrus oil. Avoid before sun exposure.
Cooling but irritating essential oil.
Strongly aromatic essential oil, irritating to sensitive skin.
Creates a cooling sensation that is often mistaken for efficacy. Irritating to compromised skin.
Counter-irritant with a cooling effect. Best avoided on sensitive skin.
Harsh cleansing surfactant that strips the barrier. Rare in modern facial cleansers.
Milder than SLS but still a stripping surfactant for dry or sensitive skin.
Gentle amphoteric surfactant used in low-irritation cleansers.
Sugar-derived non-ionic surfactant, very mild.
Gentle plant-derived surfactant for sensitive-skin cleansers.
Creamy, mild surfactant common in syndet cleansing bars.
Amino-acid surfactant that cleanses at low pH without stripping.
The most widely used modern preservative. Well tolerated at regulated levels.
Skin-conditioning agent that boosts preservative efficacy.
Preservative used alongside phenoxyethanol.
Food-grade preservative effective in acidic formulas.
Mild preservative usually paired with sodium benzoate.
Well-studied preservative considered safe at cosmetic levels, though avoided by many brands for marketing reasons.
Paraben preservative, safe at regulated concentrations.
Binds metal ions so preservatives and actives stay stable.
Natural polysaccharide thickener.
Synthetic gelling agent that gives gels their bounce.
A fatty alcohol, not a drying one. Thickens and softens creams.
Emollient fatty alcohol used to build cream textures.
Fatty acid that thickens and stabilises emulsions.
Common emulsifier and emollient in moisturizers.
Helps disperse oils and fragrance into water-based formulas.
The base of nearly every skincare formula.
European labelling term for water.
Multitasker that hydrates lightly and boosts preservative performance. Very common in K-beauty formulas.
Isomer notation for butylene glycol - a lightweight humectant and solvent.
Binds metal ions so the formula stays stable. Used at fractions of a percent.
Superabsorbent polymer that thickens and gives essences their slip.
Helps keep water-soluble actives evenly dispersed.
Light dry-touch ester used to make oily textures feel less heavy.
Silky synthetic ester that spreads easily without greasiness.
Suspending polymer that keeps powdered actives evenly distributed in anhydrous formulas.
Temporarily constricts blood vessels, which is why it turns up in eye products aimed at puffiness.
Traditional Korean botanical used for radiance and circulation, rich in antioxidant ginsenosides.
Doubles as a preservative and a declarable EU allergen. One of the more common fragrance sensitisers.
Faint floral fragrance component and declarable EU allergen.
Balsamic fragrance component and solvent. Declarable EU allergen.
Balsamic fragrance component and declarable EU allergen.
Cinnamon fragrance component and declarable EU allergen. A frequent cause of contact dermatitis.
Sweet balsamic fragrance component and declarable EU allergen.
Sweet hay-like fragrance component and declarable EU allergen.
Floral fragrance component and declarable EU allergen, also used as a deodorising agent.
Jasmine-like fragrance component and declarable EU allergen.
Floral fragrance component and declarable EU allergen.
Floral fragrance component and declarable EU allergen.
Sweet anise fragrance component and declarable EU allergen.
Muguet fragrance component and declarable EU allergen.
Clove-like fragrance component and declarable EU allergen. A stronger sensitiser than eugenol.
Violet fragrance component and declarable EU allergen.
Green violet-leaf fragrance component and declarable EU allergen.
Muguet fragrance component and declarable EU allergen. Banned in EU cosmetics from 2022, still found in older stock.
Muguet fragrance component and declarable EU allergen. EU-banned since 2021 after high sensitisation rates.
Mossy fragrance material and declarable EU allergen. One of the strongest fragrance sensitisers known.
Mossy fragrance material and declarable EU allergen, closely related to oakmoss.
Highly effective preservative and a major cause of contact allergy. EU-restricted to rinse-off products at low concentration.
Paired with methylisothiazolinone as Kathon CG. A potent contact sensitiser, restricted to rinse-off use in the EU.
Slowly releases formaldehyde to preserve the formula. A concern for anyone with a formaldehyde contact allergy.
Formaldehyde-releasing preservative and a recognised contact allergen.
Formaldehyde-releasing preservative. Relevant to anyone patch-test positive for formaldehyde.
The most sensitising of the formaldehyde releasers; largely phased out of modern formulas.
The fraction of lanolin responsible for most lanolin allergy. Listed separately from lanolin on many labels.
A standard patch-test allergen and one of the most common causes of cosmetic contact dermatitis.
Pine-derived resin and a frequent contact allergen, mostly encountered in masks and peel-off formulas.
UV filter and the most common photoallergen among sunscreen actives.
Wheat-derived oil. Relevant to wheat allergy, and to anyone avoiding gluten-derived ingredients topically.
Wheat-derived protein. Documented cause of contact urticaria in people with wheat allergy.
Soy-derived oil, relevant to soy allergy. Also mildly comedogenic.
Sesame-derived oil. Sesame is a major declarable food allergen and cross-reacts topically.
Tree-nut oil, relevant to anyone with a nut allergy.
Peanut-derived oil. Rare in modern skincare but a serious concern for peanut allergy.
